newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnia elections seen affecting Tribunal schedule.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia elections seen affecting Tribunal schedule.

text.p: The war crimes trial of Bosnian Serb Dusan "Dusko" Tadic resumes on Tuesday after a three week recess but key defence witnesses are unlikely to attend before Bosnia's September 14 elections, a defence lawyer said.

Michail Wladimiroff, a prominent Dutch criminal lawyer defending Tadic, said the first phase of the defence faced "organisational problems" as Bosnians go to the polls next Saturday in the first national elections since the 43-month Bosnian war ended in December 1995.

"Our witnesses will only leave after the elections -- the first batch will leave on the 15th," said Wladimiroff in an interview, adding the witnesses would back up Tadic's basic defence of mistaken identity.
"The implication is he couldn't have done it, but what they will tell the court is where they saw Dusko Tadic at that time (specified in the indictments)," said Wladimiroff.

Since early May the U.N. criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia has heard more than 70 witnesses called by the prosecution to back charges of murder, rape and torture of Moslems by Tadic in northwest Bosnia in 1992.

Wladimiroff said he was expecting to call 35 or 36 alibi witnesses to prove Tadic, a former cafe owner and karate expert, was working as a traffic policeman in Banja Luka, around 50 km (30 miles) away from the Prijedor region where he is alleged to have committed war crimes.

The impact of the upcoming elections in which nearly three million Bosnian voters, many of them refugees, go to the polls could be hard to judge, although the tribunal has facilities for testimony via video link.

"The only problem is that we can't call our witnesses to come to the Hague before the time of the elections. We don't know what is going to happen during the elections -- if problems arise in the area it might be a problem for our witnesses to leave," said Wladimiroff.
On Tuesday judges are expected to pronounce on a defence motion asking that 14 of 32 prosecution counts be dropped for lack of evidence.

Wladimiroff expects to have presented the full defence case by early November. "Then we will have closing arguments that will take another couple of days per side, then there's a period in which the court will decide the matter," he said.

Tribunal spokesman Christian Chartier declined to comment on how long the judges might deliberate in the case. If he is found guilty, they could impose a life sentence on Tadic, who has been in tribunal custody since April 1995.
So far the tribunal has indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems, but has only seven men, including Tadic, in custody.

Tadic is the first person to face an international war crimes trial since the Nuremberg and Tokyo hearings following World War Two, but Chartier said the tribunal was on course to open its second trial before the end of the year.

The most advanced case is that of former Bosnian Croat Defence Council (HVO) commander Tihomir Blaskic, held in tribunal custody on charges relating to attacks on Moslem civilians in central Bosnia, Chartier said.

Investigators exhuming mass graves in Bosnia have strengthened the tribunal's case against its two most wanted men -- deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic.
They are accused of genocide after Bosnian Serb forces stormed the U.N. "safe haven" of Srebrenica in east Bosnia in July 1995.
"What is for sure is that the findings of the diggers in the field have fully confirmed the testimony or evidence gathered by the tribunal's own investigators," said Chartier.
"We have not discovered any discrepancy. It has made the prosecution case against Karadzic and Mladic definitely stronger," he said.
